fields.name: ah
fields.label: Battery capacity
fields.hint: From the battery label, for example 100, 150 or 200 Ah.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Battery voltage
fields.hint: A single battery is 12 V; two in series make 24 V.

fields.name: psh
fields.label: Peak sun hours a day
fields.hint: Hours of full-strength sun a day. Pakistani cities get about five to six on a clear day; use four for winter or a cloudy place.

fields.name: dod
fields.label: Depth of discharge to refill
fields.hint: How much of the battery is used each day and must be put back. As a decimal; half for lead-acid, most of it for lithium.

fields.name: charge_eff
fields.label: Charging efficiency
fields.hint: Share of the energy sent in that the battery stores. Lead-acid loses more than lithium. As a decimal.

fields.name: pr
fields.label: Performance ratio
fields.hint: Share of the panel's rated watts you really get after heat, dust, wiring and controller losses. As a decimal.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Charge controller margin
fields.hint: Sizing margin on the controller current. A decimal like one point two five.

answer: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery needs at least a {{out.panel_w|int}} W solar panel to put back half its charge in {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours, so buy a {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel with a {{out.standard_controller_a|int}} A MPPT charge controller. That panel refills the battery in about {{out.charge_hours|1}} hours of peak sun. Panel watts = Ah × V × depth of discharge ÷ charging efficiency ÷ (sun hours × performance ratio).
how: Energy to put back: {{in.ah|int}} Ah × {{in.volts|int}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} depth of discharge ÷ {{out.charge_eff|pct}} charging efficiency = the watt-hours the panel must deliver. Divided by {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours × {{out.pr|2}} performance ratio = {{out.panel_w|int}} W minimum, rounded up to the next panel size sold, {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W. That panel refills the battery in {{out.charge_hours|1}} hours of peak sun, about {{out.charge_days|1}} sunny days. Controller: {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W ÷ {{in.volts|int}} V × {{d.margin|2}} margin = {{out.controller_a|1}} A, so a {{out.standard_controller_a|int}} A MPPT controller.
key_facts: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery used to {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} needs a {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W solar panel ({{out.panel_w|int}} W minimum) to recharge in {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours.

A {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery needs a {{ex.1.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel and a {{ex.1.out.standard_controller_a|int}} A MPPT controller under the same sun; doubling the Ah doubles the panel watts.

Solar panel watts to charge a battery = Ah × V × depth of discharge ÷ charging efficiency ÷ (peak sun hours × performance ratio); a panel rarely gives its label watts, so the {{d.pr|2}} ratio matters.

Lead-acid batteries store about {{d.charge_eff_lead_acid|pct}} of the energy sent in and should be refilled from about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}}; lithium stores about {{d.charge_eff_lifepo4|pct}} and can be used to {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}}, so a {{ex.3.in.ah|int}} Ah lithium battery needs a {{ex.3.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel.

formula.text: W = (Ah × V × DoD ÷ η_chg) ÷ (PSH × PR); t = (Ah × V × DoD ÷ η_chg) ÷ (W_fitted × PR); A = W_fitted ÷ V × m
lines: W = minimum panel watts; W_fitted = the next panel size sold
Ah, V = battery capacity and voltage
DoD = depth of discharge to put back each day
η_chg = charging efficiency of the battery
PSH = peak sun hours a day; PR = performance ratio
t = hours of peak sun to a full charge
A = MPPT controller current; m = margin

sections.h2: What size solar panel do I need to charge a {{in.volts|int}} V battery?
p: Work out the energy to put back, then divide by what a panel really delivers. A {{in.ah|int}} Ah {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery used to {{out.dod|pct}} needs {{in.ah|int}} × {{in.volts|int}} × {{out.dod|pct}} watt-hours, plus the charging loss ({{out.charge_eff|pct}} efficiency). Over {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours at a performance ratio of {{out.pr|2}}, that comes to {{out.panel_w|int}} W, so the panel to buy is {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W.

The calculator rounds up to the next panel size sold. If the rounding gives you a much bigger panel than the minimum, the charge simply finishes sooner: the time to a full charge is shown for the panel you buy, not for the minimum watts.

sections.h2: Solar panel for a {{ex.0.in.ah|int}} Ah battery and a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery
p: For a {{ex.0.in.ah|int}} Ah {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery with {{ex.0.in.psh|int}} peak sun hours the minimum is {{ex.0.out.panel_w|int}} W, so a {{ex.0.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel with a {{ex.0.out.standard_controller_a|int}} A MPPT controller. For a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery the minimum is {{ex.1.out.panel_w|int}} W, so a {{ex.1.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel and a {{ex.1.out.standard_controller_a|int}} A controller.

These sizes refill a battery used to half each day. If you only use a quarter of the battery, lower the depth of discharge in the advanced options and the panel halves; if you want a day's charge back from a deeper discharge, raise it.

sections.h2: Which charge controller for a {{in.volts|int}} V battery: MPPT or PWM?
p: The controller current shown is for an MPPT controller: panel watts ÷ battery volts × a {{d.margin|2}} margin, rounded up to the next size sold, {{out.standard_controller_a|int}} A for the {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel on a {{in.volts|int}} V battery. An MPPT controller converts the panel's higher voltage into charging current, so a higher-voltage panel still delivers its full watts.

A PWM controller is cheaper but wastes the difference between the panel voltage and the battery voltage, so it only works well with a panel made for the battery's voltage and delivers noticeably less than the calculator assumes. If you use PWM, buy a bigger panel or expect slower charging. The charge controller calculator covers PWM sizing by panel current.

sections.h2: Solar charging time calculator: how long to charge the battery?
p: With the panel you buy, the battery refills in {{out.charge_hours|1}} hours of peak sun, which is {{out.charge_days|1}} days at {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours a day. Peak sun hours are not daylight hours: a Pakistani summer day has far more daylight than its five to six peak sun hours, because morning and evening sun is weak.

Lead-acid batteries also slow down in the last part of the charge (the absorption stage), so the real time to a truly full battery is longer than this estimate. Treat it as the time to put back the day's energy, not as a stopwatch.

mistakes: Using daylight hours instead of peak sun hours. A twelve-hour day gives only about five to six hours of full-strength sun, so a panel sized on daylight hours is far too small.
Expecting the label watts from the panel. Heat, dust, cable loss and the controller take their share; the calculator keeps only {{d.pr|pct}} of the rating.
Matching panel watts to battery Ah with no sun or depth figure. A battery used to a quarter and one drained every day need very different panels for the same Ah.
Using a PWM controller with a high-voltage panel. It clips the panel to the battery voltage and loses a large part of the watts; the controller current here is for MPPT.
Skipping the controller altogether. A panel wired straight to a battery overcharges it once it is full and shortens its life.
safety: Fuse the battery and the panel cable, use a charge controller rated for the panel, keep lead-acid batteries ventilated, and have a licensed electrician or certified installer wire any system that feeds house circuits.

faq.q: What size solar panel do I need for a {{ex.0.in.ah|int}} Ah battery?
faq.a: A {{ex.0.in.ah|int}} Ah {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery used to half needs a {{ex.0.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel ({{ex.0.out.panel_w|int}} W minimum) with {{ex.0.in.psh|int}} peak sun hours a day, and refills in about {{ex.0.out.charge_hours|1}} hours of peak sun.

faq.q: What size solar panel for a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery?
faq.a: A {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery needs a {{ex.1.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel ({{ex.1.out.panel_w|int}} W minimum) and a {{ex.1.out.standard_controller_a|int}} A MPPT charge controller to put back half its charge in {{ex.1.in.psh|int}} peak sun hours.

faq.q: How many watts does it take to charge a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery?
faq.a: The energy is {{in.ah|int}} Ah × {{in.volts|int}} V × the share you used; at {{out.dod|pct}} with charging losses the panel must deliver about {{out.panel_w|int}} W over {{in.psh|int}} peak sun hours. Any panel from {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W up does it; a bigger panel only charges faster, as long as the controller is rated for it.

faq.q: Which charge controller do I need for a {{in.volts|int}} V battery?
faq.a: An MPPT controller rated for the panel watts ÷ battery volts with a {{d.margin|2}} margin: {{out.standard_controller_a|int}} A for a {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel on a {{in.volts|int}} V battery. Also check the controller's maximum panel voltage against the panel's open-circuit voltage.

faq.q: How long does a solar panel take to charge a {{in.volts|int}} V battery?
faq.a: The {{out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel refills a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery used to {{out.dod|pct}} in about {{out.charge_hours|1}} hours of peak sun, roughly {{out.charge_days|1}} sunny days. Cloud, a dirty panel or a PWM controller make it longer, and lead-acid batteries slow down near full.

faq.q: Is the panel size different for a lithium battery?
faq.a: The formula is the same but the numbers differ: lithium charges at about {{d.charge_eff_lifepo4|pct}} efficiency and is used to about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}}, so a {{ex.3.in.ah|int}} Ah lithium battery used fully each day needs a {{ex.3.out.standard_panel_w|int}} W panel. Set the depth of discharge and charging efficiency in the advanced options.

faq.q: Can I connect a solar panel straight to a {{in.volts|int}} V battery?
faq.a: Not for daily use. Without a charge controller the panel keeps pushing current into a full battery and boils the electrolyte or damages the cells. Even a small panel should go through a controller.
